mappings.note: Dehydration of ethanol with conditions and the role of conc. H2SO4 (LO-8), plus the structure of X and the electron dot structure of the ethene formed (C 1.3-LO-4). The '-ol' suffix is only a clue, so C 1.1-LO-4 is not added.

Four parts, three targets: dehydration and esterification are LO-8; sorting the four formulae into saturated hydrocarbon and organic acid is C 1.1-LO-4; the structural formula of ethanoic acid is C 1.3-LO-4.

Three unrelated parts: (a) addition/bromine-water identification of ethene (C 1.3, no outcome for addition); (b) structural formulae of butanone and pentanoic acid (C 1.3-LO-4); (c) whether a detergent can test hardness (C 1.2-LO-9).
Composition and hard-water behaviour of soaps against detergents - LO-9 covers the whole item on its own.
Part (a) names the four-carbon alcohol and aldehyde (C 1.1-LO-4) and demands their structures (C 1.3-LO-4); part (b), saturated versus unsaturated, is a series distinction that rides with LO-4.

Three separate demands: the electron dot structure of methane (C 1.3-LO-4), the functional groups in C2H6O and C2H4O (C 1.1-LO-4), and why ethyne is burnt in oxygen rather than air, which is a combustion question with no outcome (C 1.3).
Conversions (i) and (iii) are ethanol oxidation and esterification (LO-8); conversion (ii) is hydrogenation of ethene (C 1.3); part (b) asks why detergents are preferred (LO-9).

Part (a) is why carbon bonds covalently and the two reasons for so many compounds - LO-3 exactly. Part (b), the formation of ammonia, is a non-carbon molecule and so falls outside C 1.3-LO-4's wording, taking C 1.1 instead.

Bromine-water test, combustion of ethane, and why methane with chlorine is a substitution. All three parts are reaction types or combustion, none of which has an outcome, so one competency-level code covers the item.
General formulae of the three series (C 1.1-LO-4), structures of their first members (C 1.3-LO-4), and naming plus equating the alkene-to-alkane hydrogenation (C 1.3).
Soap/detergent difference, the micelle mechanism of cleansing, failure in hard water and the problems detergents cause - every clause of LO-9 in one item.
Part (a) contrasts esterification with saponification, both named in LO-8; part (b) asks the advantages of detergents over soaps, which is LO-9.
Defines covalent compounds, contrasts them with ionic ones and lists three properties. The frame's clearest content gap: no outcome covers covalent-compound properties, so the competency carries it.

Identifies ethanoic acid from the carbonate effervescence, tests the gas, writes the equation and lists uses - all properties of the named acid, LO-8. The lime-water test is subordinate, so C 1.3 is not added.
Part (a) is catenation and tetravalency (LO-3); parts (b) and (c) turn on saturation and comparative reactivity, which is reaction behaviour (C 1.3); part (d) demands two structures (C 1.3-LO-4).
Three reactions of ethanoic acid, the role of conc. H2SO4 in esterification, and one use - LO-8 throughout.
Ethanoic acid identified as the pickle preservative, then esterification, recovery by saponification and the washing-soda reaction - all LO-8 content.
Distinguishing ethanol from ethanoic acid by carbonate, plus reasons for their uses - a direct contrast of the two compounds LO-8 names.
Part (a) is ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate (LO-8); part (b) asks the names of bromoethane and propene, which is nomenclature (C 1.1-LO-4) and unrelated to the first half.

Three targets: ethanol's dehydration and the weak-acid nature of carboxylic acids (LO-8); which compounds undergo substitution (C 1.3); and the electron dot formation of O2, a non-carbon molecule outside C 1.3-LO-4's wording (C 1.1).
A is identified through ethanol's dehydration (LO-8); the hydrogenation to ethane and the combustion stoichiometry that fixes C are reaction types with no outcome (C 1.3).
Five-step sequence built entirely from ethanol and ethanoic acid chemistry - oxidation, esterification, saponification, bicarbonate and sodium. One LO-8 code carries all of it.
Five equations, every one a reaction of ethanol (combustion, sodium, oxidation, esterification, dehydration). All are properties of the named compound, so no C 1.3 code is needed.
Reactions (i), (ii) and (v) are ethanol and ethanoic acid chemistry (LO-8); (iii) chlorination of methane and (iv) hydrogenation of ethene have no outcome and take C 1.3.
Part (a) asks for the structural formulae of the alcohol and acid behind an ester (C 1.3-LO-4); part (b) asks the conditions and equation for ethanol's dehydration (LO-8).
